paragraphs: R' Shimon ben Halafta: Uktzin, chapter 3, mishnah 12.

1. It appears that he was R' Yosa ben Halafta's younger brother. See Mo'ed Katan 9b: he took leave of Rabbi and blessed Rabbi's son in the Ein Yaakov text. The compared Bavli reads Rav. Rashi in Ein Yaakov writes that he was Rabbi's pupil and an amora, whereas R' Yose ben Halafta was a tanna. End of quotation. None of this is in Rashi in the Gemara. Yuhasin brings him in the order of the tannaim, and he is right, since he is mentioned in the Mishnah. In Shabbat, Sho'el, 152a, Rabbi said to him, “Why have we not received your presence at the festival as my forebears received your forebears?” Rashi: “You have not received my presence”; he speaks to him respectfully. He answered, “Those who were near have become distant ….” He told him that it was because of old age. So too in Midrash Rabbah, Metzora, chapter 18; Kohelet, at “Also from a height”; and Rabbah, Tzav, chapter 10. Antoninus sent to Rabbi, “You said that the least of your pupils revives the dead. Send me one of your pupils, for my slave is near death.” He sent him one of his pupils; some say it was R' Shimon ben Halafta. He went and found the slave lying in bed and said, “Why are you lying down while I stand over you?” Immediately he arose. In Ruth Rabbah, at “She arose to glean”: Rabbi used to declare grain heaps ownerless so that R' Shimon ben Halafta might acquire them.

2. He investigated things: with a hen whose feathers had been removed, to disprove R' Yehudah's view; and he tested Shelomoh's words about the ant, that it has no chief, officer, or ruler. He had a hen whose thigh had slipped out; he made it a tube of reed, and it lived: Hullin 57b. Lions encountered him and roared at him. Two haunches descended. In the Bavli, the lions ate one and left one. He asked in the study hall whether it was permissible to eat, and they told him, “Nothing impure descends from heaven”: Sanhedrin 59b. He did not have a doubt about slaughter, because, since it had not been created from a father and mother, it did not need slaughter: ענ״ב [unresolved work; E.N.B.], section 125, and my large work. In Shemot Rabbah, chapter 52—and in Midrash Ruth, at “Where you die I shall die,” somewhat differently—a pearl was given to him from heaven and he returned it. The latter is even greater than the former, for from heaven they give but do not take.

In Kohelet Rabbah, at “A time to be born”: R' Shimon ben Halafta came to a town, where youths were playing before a courtyard. They said, “Do not move from here until you dance a little for us.” He said, “I am an old man.” He rebuked them, but they did not submit to him. He said, “Repeat after me what I say,” and sang, “Tell the owner of the courtyard to shake himself awake, for in the end it will be bitter for him.” That is, the youths' misconduct depended on him, because he had not taught them discipline. He awoke from his sleep, fell at R' Shimon ben Halafta's feet, and asked him not to heed their words, for they were young and foolish. He said, “What can I do? The decree has already been issued that the courtyard shall fall. But I shall do this for you: it will not fall until you remove everything in the courtyard.” Immediately after he cleared it, it fell. From there he went with the townspeople to the commandment of circumcision. The infant's father gave them wine and said, “Drink! I trust in the Lord that from this wine I shall serve you at his wedding.” After he left there for his own town, the Angel of Death met him and said, “Because you trust in your good deeds, you go out at night, when harmful spirits are common.” R' Shimon asked, “Why is your face so troubled?” He answered, “Because of the things I hear from people's mouths.” “What are they?” He said, “The infant circumcised today: his sentence is with me, that I should take him after thirty days. Yet I heard his father express confidence that he would serve wine from that same wine at his wedding. Therefore I am sad, for I fear that this prayer he uttered will annul the decree.” R' Shimon said, “Please show me when my appointed time is.” He answered, “I have no control over the time of yours or of people like you.” He said, “May it be His will: just as you have no control over my time, so may you have no permission to transgress these words of ours.” He sought mercy, and the infant lived. So too in Rabbah, beginning of Vayelekh. He was corpulent: I did not find this. Another reading names the corpulent man as R' Yishmael son of R' Yose, with “his brother” in the Hebrew.

3. In Abba the Expositor's name. R' Abba bar Zavda reports in his name. R' Hunya of the house of Havran reports in his name. R' Hiyya the Great called him “Beribbi” and reports in his name: Shir ha-Shirim Rabbah, Ruth, and Megillah. R' Simon reports in his name: Shir ha-Shirim Rabbah.
